source_refs.note: Book p. 18: 1.7 definition, examples, V-shaped graph, Figure 1.12

blocks.text: The modulus function or absolute value function is denoted and defined by:

blocks.text_alt: f of x equals modulus of x, which is x when x is greater than or equal to 0, and minus x when x is less than 0

blocks.text: For example, if \(x = 2 > 0\) then \(|x| = |2| = 2\) and if \(x = -2 < 0\) then \(|x| = |-2| = -(-2) = 2\). Similarly, \(x = 0\) then \(|x| = |0| = 0\). Thus, the modulus of a number is always non-negative.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The rule \(|x| = -x\) for \(x < 0\) often confuses students, because of the minus sign. But if \(x\) is negative, then \(-x\) is positive: \(-(-2) = 2\). Think of \(|x|\) as the distance of \(x\) from 0 on the number line; a distance is never negative, and \(-2\) and \(2\) are both 2 units from 0.

The graph of the modulus function is V-shaped. It consists of two straight lines meeting at the origin. For \(x \ge 0\), the graph is the line \(y = x\), while for \(x < 0\), the graph is the line \(y = -x\). Thus, the graph of modulus function can be sketched using the points \((0, 0)\), \((2, 2)\) and \((-2, 2)\) as shown in Figure 1.12.

blocks.alt: Grid graph on a pale yellow panel, x from minus 4 to 5 and y from 0 to 6, labelled f(x) = |x|. Two blue rays with arrows form a V with its corner at the origin. The dots (minus 2, 2), (2, 2) and (0, 0) are marked; a small arrow points to (0, 0).
blocks.caption: Figure 1.12: graph of the modulus function f(x) = |x| (original drawing after the textbook's figure)
Teaching note: our value table for f(x) = |x| (not printed in the book)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What the graph shows (our summary):
1. Domain \(\mathbb{R}\), range \([0, \infty[\): the graph never goes below the \(x\)-axis.
2. It is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, since \(|-x| = |x|\).
3. Its lowest point (vertex) is the origin \((0, 0)\); there the graph has a sharp corner.
4. It is continuous: the two lines meet at the origin, so there is no gap.
5. It is not one-to-one, since \(|-2| = |2| = 2\): the horizontal line \(y = 2\) meets it twice. You will need this idea in 1.8.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(|x| = x\) for \(x \ge 0\) and \(|x| = -x\) for \(x < 0\).
2. \(|x| \ge 0\) for every real \(x\).
3. The graph is a V made of \(y = -x\) (left) and \(y = x\) (right), vertex at \((0, 0)\).
4. Three points are enough to sketch it: \((-2, 2)\), \((0, 0)\), \((2, 2)\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(|x| = -x\) as 'the modulus is negative'. For \(x < 0\), \(-x\) is positive.
2. Drawing the left arm below the \(x\)-axis (that is the graph of \(y = x\), not \(|x|\)).
3. Rounding the corner at the origin into a curve: the two arms are straight lines.
